title: Better Genetic Risk Scores for Autism and Other Neuropsychiatric Conditions
summary: Reticular combines common and rare genetic variants to capture information that a common-variant polygenic score can miss.
body_markdown:
Reticular's genetic scores help identify people with greater genetic susceptibility to certain conditions from their DNA. By combining common and rare DNA variants, we’ve improved our genetic risk scores for four neuropsychiatric conditions: autism, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and intellectual disability. In a large research study, diagnoses were more common in the highest-scoring 5% for each combined score than in the top 5% ranked by common variants alone.


## Diagnosis rates reached about 4x the study average


For each condition, we ranked the same participants using the common-variant-only score and the combined score, then examined each score’s highest-scoring 5%. The combined score identified groups with higher recorded diagnosis frequencies:


- **Intellectual disability:** about 4× as often as average, up from 2.4× before
- **Autism:** about 2× as often, up from 1.3×
- **Schizophrenia:** about 2× as often, up from 1.3×
- **Bipolar disorder:** about 1.7× as often, up from 1.5×


**Recorded diagnoses across the genetic-score range.** Gray shows the common-variant-only score; plum shows the combined score. A value of 1× represents the study average. Shading marks the top 5%; error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Panels use different vertical scales.


## More people with a diagnosis ranked in the top 5%


Another way to look at it: of everyone with a diagnosis, how many did each score place in its top 5%? For autism, the combined score placed about 1 in 10 people in this group, up from about 1 in 16 using common variants alone. Schizophrenia showed a similar increase. For intellectual disability, the share rose to about 1 in 5, up from about 1 in 8. Bipolar disorder improved more modestly.


**The combined score places a larger share of diagnosed participants within its highest-scoring 5%.** Bars show the percentage of all participants with each recorded diagnosis who fall in that score group. Differences are expressed in percentage points and calculated before rounding. These percentages describe existing diagnoses in the study cohorts.


## What changed


Traditional polygenic scores mainly use common DNA differences with small individual effects. Our new scores also include selected rare variants, which are uncommon but can have larger effects. We use genomic AI to help prioritize additional rare variants that may affect biological function. For details on the rare-variant approach and the common-variant scores used in each analysis, read our[technical companion post](https://reticular.com/blog/genomic-ai-rare-missense) .


**The combined score brings together common and rare DNA variants.** Genomic AI helps prioritize additional rare variants alongside those already included.


## What this means for your family


A genetic score estimates risk. It isn't a diagnosis. A higher score means higher odds of a condition, not a certainty, and many people with these conditions don't have high scores. Genetics is also only part of the picture: environment and chance matter too. Our genetic counselors can walk you through what a score means for your family.


## About this analysis


These results describe recorded diagnoses in adults of European ancestry in the All of Us Research Program. They evaluate the full combined score, not genomic AI alone, and do not estimate individual lifetime risk. Performance in children and other populations requires further validation. These figures use an updated common-variant baseline covering approximately 7.7 million variants, compared with approximately 1 million in the[technical companion post](https://reticular.com/blog/genomic-ai-rare-missense) . Both the common-variant-only and combined scores use this updated baseline. We gratefully acknowledge All of Us participants for their contributions, without whom this research would not have been possible. We also thank the National Institutes of Health’s All of Us Research Program for making available the participant data examined in this study.
